title: Decimal Operations Grade 5: Add, Subtract, Multiply & Divide (Free Quiz)
meta_title: Decimal Operations Grade 5: The 4 Skills + Quiz
meta_desc: Grade 5 decimal operations made simple: line up the point to add and subtract, count places to multiply, divide by 10, 100 and 1000. Free quiz inside.
excerpt: Most Grade 5 decimal mistakes come from one habit: not lining up the point. Here is how to add, subtract, multiply and divide decimals cleanly, with an 8-question quiz to check.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 5 class 3.5 + 12 and watch what happens. A good third of them will write the 12 under the 5, add, and confidently report 3.7. The answer is 15.5, of course — but the error is not about decimals being hard. It is about one habit that decides everything else: lining up the decimal point. Once children treat decimal operations grade 5 as ‘the same arithmetic, just keep the points in a column,’ the whole topic settles down. This post walks through the four skills your child actually needs — adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing decimals — with the exact traps to watch for in each.

I am assuming your child already knows what a decimal is (that 0.7 means seven tenths). This is about doing things with decimals, not naming the places. If the naming is still shaky, sort that first — the operations lean on it.

Adding and subtracting: the decimal point rules everything

The single rule for adding or subtracting decimals is to stack the numbers so the decimal points sit in one straight vertical line. Not the last digits — the points. Everything else is ordinary column addition your child has done since Grade 2.

The classic disaster is a number like 12 that seems to have no decimal point. It does: 12 is 12.0, and you can add as many trailing zeros as you need. So 3.5 + 12 becomes 3.5 + 12.0, points lined up, and the answer is 15.5.

Filling the gaps with zeros

When the numbers have different numbers of decimal places, pad the shorter one with zeros so both are the same length. To work out 4.6 − 1.25, rewrite 4.6 as 4.60 first. Now it is 4.60 − 1.25 = 3.35. Skipping that zero is where the borrowing goes wrong.

  • Line up the decimal points vertically, not the right-hand edge.
  • Give a whole number its point and a zero: 7 becomes 7.0.
  • Pad shorter decimals with trailing zeros so both match.
  • Bring the decimal point straight down into the answer.

Multiplying decimals: forget the point, then count

Here is the counter-intuitive part, and it is the one that surprises parents. When you multiply decimals, you do not line up the points. You ignore the points entirely, multiply as if they were whole numbers, and only at the very end count how many decimal places to put back.

The count is simple: add up the number of decimal places in both numbers, and the answer has that many. For 0.6 × 0.7, ignore the points and do 6 × 7 = 42. Each number had one decimal place, so the answer has two: 0.42. Notice the answer is smaller than either number — multiplying by a number less than one shrinks things. That trips up children who expect ‘times makes bigger,’ so name it out loud.

Dividing by a whole number: point goes straight up

Dividing a decimal by a whole number is the friendliest of the four. Set up long division exactly as normal, and put the decimal point in the answer directly above the point in the number you are dividing. Then divide digit by digit as usual.

So 7.5 ÷ 3: the point in the answer sits above the point in 7.5, then 7 ÷ 3 and carry, giving 2.5. If a digit will not divide, add a zero after the decimal and keep going — 9.6 ÷ 5 needs one extra zero to finish as 1.92. My one piece of advice: make your child write the point first, before dividing a single digit. Placing it afterwards is how the answer ends up ten times too big or too small.

Dividing by 10, 100 and 1000: just slide the point

This last skill looks like a shortcut but it is really the heart of the whole place-value system. To divide by 10, 100 or 1000, you do not do long division at all — you slide the decimal point to the left by one place for each zero.

  • 45.6 ÷ 10 → point moves 1 left → 4.56
  • 45.6 ÷ 100 → point moves 2 left → 0.456
  • 45.6 ÷ 1000 → point moves 3 left → 0.0456

When you run out of digits, fill in with zeros — that is why 45.6 ÷ 1000 needs a leading zero. Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1000 is the mirror image: the point slides right. Get your child to say ‘dividing makes it smaller, so the point goes left’ each time, until the direction is automatic.

A quick word on estimating first

Before your child computes anything, get them to guess roughly. 3.5 + 12 is ‘about 15,’ so an answer of 3.7 is obviously wrong. 0.6 × 0.7 is ‘less than one,’ so 42 cannot be right without the point. Estimation is the cheapest error-check there is, and it costs five seconds. In my experience it catches more mistakes than any amount of re-checking the arithmetic.

quiz.intro: Eight questions on adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing decimals. Work each one out, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Write 12 as 12.0 and line up the points: 3.5 + 12.0 = 15.5.
Pad 4.6 to 4.60, line up the points, then subtract: 4.60 − 1.25 = 3.35.
Ignore the points: 6 × 7 = 42. There are 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places, so the answer is 0.42.
25 × 4 = 100, and there is 1 decimal place in total, so the answer is 10.0 = 10.
Put the point in the answer above the point in 7.5, then divide: 7.5 ÷ 3 = 2.5.
Dividing by 10 slides the point one place left: 45.6 becomes 4.56.
Dividing by 100 slides the point two places left: 45.6 becomes 0.456.
5 × 6 = 30, and there are 2 decimal places, so the answer is 0.30.

faq.q: Why do you line up decimals to add but not to multiply?
faq.a: Adding and subtracting combine numbers place by place, so tenths must sit under tenths — that only works if the points are in a column. Multiplying does not combine like places; you multiply the digits and then count the total decimal places at the end, so lining up the points is unnecessary.

faq.q: How does my child know where the decimal point goes when multiplying?
faq.a: Count the decimal places in both numbers and add them together. The answer has that many decimal places. For 1.2 × 0.3 there is one place plus one place, so the answer 0.36 has two places.

faq.q: What is the easiest way to divide by 10, 100 or 1000?
faq.a: Slide the decimal point to the left — one place for 10, two for 100, three for 1000. If you run out of digits, fill the gaps with zeros. For example, 45.6 ÷ 1000 = 0.0456.

faq.q: My child keeps getting answers ten times too big. What is going wrong?
faq.a: Usually the decimal point in a division answer is placed last, or forgotten. Teach them to write the point in the answer first — directly above the point in the number being divided — before dividing any digits.
